newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria sells stakes in 587 firms for vouchers.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria sells stakes in 587 firms for vouchers.

text.p: More than half of Bulgarian state enterprises earmarked for privatisation have passed into private ownership after the second mass sell-off, a government official said on Tuesday.

"The majority of the capital of 587 enterprises of a total of 1,050 listed (for mass privatisation) is now privately-owned," Mass Privatisation Center director Pirin Atanasov said at a news conference.
In 439 state firms the private share was more than 67 percent, he added.
Under Bulgaria's mass privatisation programme launched last year to speed up restructuring, some 1,050 enterprises with capital of around 95 billion levs were offered for mass sell-offs.
Around three million Bulgarians or almost half of the eligible population bought voucher booklets, each with a face value of 25,000 levs, which enabled them to take part in the programme.
They participated directly in the auctions, through the local post stations, or through 81 privatisation funds approved by the Stock Exchange and Securities Commission.
In the second voucher tender, which ended in April, 54.374 million shares in 820 firms were offered of which 24.187 million shares were bought.
Privatisation funds and individuals took part in the second tender, spending 14.3 billion levs worth of vouchers out of an available 23.6 billion levs.
Voucher capital of 9.3 billion levs remained for the third tender, where 30.187 million shares remaining from the first and second tenders will be offered.
Shares in seven new companies will also be available, taking the total number of firms set for mass privatisation to 1,057.

The third tender is due to be held later this year, Atanasov said. The enterprises scheduled for mass privatisation included metal smelters, chemical fertiliser producers, a tyre maker and food processing plants.
Shares left over after the third tender are expected to be collected in a post-privatisation fund, which will be mostly privately-owned, Atanasov said.
The European Bank for Reconstruction and Development has proposed backing for such a fund.
